clue.text: Cain or Abel on the road?

definitions.note: a cryptic gloss: the surface that is on a road

wordplay.note: Mac in a surname means son of, and each brother was a son of the first man in Genesis

explanation.surface: A biblical brother, either the murderer or the victim, out travelling.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mac- prefix of Scottish surnames means 'son of', and Genesis makes both brothers sons of the first man. The road surface is named after its inventor, John McAdam.
explanation.definitionFit: Macadam is a layered crushed-stone paving, so it is what lies under travellers along a highway.

clue.text: Graham swilling tonic instead of gin?

parts.note: the surname of a famous American modern-dance choreographer
a teasing hint at a cocktail name altered by swapping its spirit for a soft mixer

explanation.surface: Someone called Graham drinking a soft mixer rather than the hard stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: Martha Graham was the pioneering American modern dancer. The rest plays on MARTini, a gin cocktail, losing its gin for something milder; the exact letter mechanics are loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Martha was the given name of the celebrated choreographer Graham, founder of an American dance company.

clue.text: Do rough repair on stone

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to mend clumsily or patch together
second meaning: a small rounded paving stone

explanation.surface: Patching up a piece of masonry in a hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: To cobble is to mend roughly, as a cobbler patches shoes, and a cobble is a rounded paving stone.

clue.text: Girl provided 12 after a month to muddle the small ads?

definitions.note: a cryptic, infinitive gloss on the verb

indicators.note: one thing after another comes second, so the girl and the rest follow the month

parts.note: short for December
a girl, especially in Scotland and the north of England
provided that = if
the answer to 12 across is a unit of length, abbreviated Y

explanation.surface: A girl messing up the classified columns of a newspaper a month later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After a month' puts the month first. The definition is a pun: small ads are 'classified', so muddling their order would un-classify them.
explanation.definitionFit: To declassify normally means releasing secret papers; here it is jokingly read as undoing the sorting of classified advertisements.

clue.text: Polo competition starts — no score after a month

parts.note: short for March

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: opening letter of the word
a nil score, written as zero

explanation.surface: A polo match begins with neither side scoring for a month.
explanation.walkthrough: Polo is not the game but the Venetian traveller, so the answer is his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Marco is the given name of Polo, the medieval Venetian merchant who journeyed to China.

clue.text: Unaware 1 pound is missing, that's clear

indicators.note: something missing has been taken out, so those letters drop away

parts.note: unaware = oblivious
the digit read as the Roman numeral
L for pound sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Someone who has not noticed a pound coin has gone; that much is plain.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the L and I from OBLIVIOUS to leave OBVIOUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obvious is plain to see, evident and unmistakable, hence clear.

clue.text: Musical version of 24 23

definitions.note: adjective in the clue for a noun answer: a musical body

indicators.note: a version is a rendering that reworks the original, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the linked answer to 24 and 23 down

explanation.surface: A stage-musical adaptation of a story about a draught animal.
explanation.walkthrough: CART HORSE and ORCHESTRA are a famous perfect anagram pair.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchestra is a large ensemble of instrumental players, the musical body of a concert hall.

clue.text: 1 down's island is 5 in English measure
Musical time kept by viewer

indicators.note: something kept by another is held inside its keeper

parts.note: an optic is an eye or lens, something that views
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: Someone watching keeps the beat of a song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musical' looks like a show, but here it is an adjective; 'kept by' has the eye-related word holding the period.
explanation.definitionFit: Operatic means relating to opera, the sung dramatic form, so it is an adjective for something musical.

clue.text: Way to apply rouge to both sides at once?

definitions.note: a cryptic gloss for the verb: to sit on both sides

parts.note: abbreviation of street
to raddle is to colour with red ochre or rouge

explanation.surface: A make-up tip for reddening both cheeks in one go.
explanation.walkthrough: Raddle is red ochre, used to mark sheep, and as a verb means to paint with rouge.
explanation.definitionFit: To straddle is to sit or stand with legs on either side of something, being on two sides simultaneously.

clue.text: Painter using ballpoint afflicted with hydrophobia

parts.note: Royal Academician
the familiar brand of ballpoint pen

explanation.surface: An artist working with a cheap biro who is terrified of water.
explanation.definitionFit: Hydrophobia is an old name for rabies, and rabic is the adjective for that disease.

clue.text: Telltale disturbance of our trance

indicators.note: disturbing things throws them out of order, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: the fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Someone who informs on others breaks the spell we were under.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Telltale' looks like an informer, but it is read as one who tells tales.
explanation.definitionFit: A raconteur is a skilled storyteller, literally someone who tells tales to an audience.

clue.text: See 18
See 6
A Monday off, bearing 067 degrees, rising like Venus from the sea

definitions.text: rising like Venus from the sea

indicators.note: something off has gone wrong or out of kilter, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the fodder, seven letters
east-north-east is the compass bearing of 67.5 degrees

explanation.surface: A day off work, heading roughly east-north-east, emerging like the goddess from the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: Anadyomene is a Greek epithet of Aphrodite, 'she who rises from the sea', as in Botticelli's Birth of Venus.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek epithet means emerging upward from water, the classical title of the goddess born of sea foam.

clue.text: Solid vehicle returned to street, not by a pro, by a learner

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the word is read right to left

parts.note: a bus is a road vehicle
standard abbreviation
someone who is not pro something is against it
taken as written
L-plate for a learner driver

explanation.surface: A sturdy van sent back to the road, driven not by a professional but by a learner.
explanation.walkthrough: SUB, ST, ANTI, A, L. The surface makes 'pro' a professional driver; it is the opposite of anti.
explanation.definitionFit: Substantial means sturdy, solidly built and of real substance, so it is a synonym of solid.

clue.text: Sore feet in bed did well

indicators.note: something sore is in a bad way, so the following letters are shaken up

parts.note: the fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Aching feet tucked up in bed got better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sore feet' reads as one phrase, but 'Sore' is the anagram signal and 'in' is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To have benefited is to have gained or profited from something, past tense matching the clue.

clue.text: Linguistic line: that's how I put on top coat

parts.note: taken as written
so = in that way
to gloss is to apply a shiny finishing coat

explanation.surface: A painter explaining a technique: that's the way I do the final layer.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface looks like decorating, though an isogloss is a technical term from dialect geography.
explanation.definitionFit: An isogloss is a boundary on a dialect map separating areas that differ in some speech feature.

clue.text: University parallel to the pons asinorum?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the blend name for the two oldest English universities
second meaning: the pons asinorum is the bridge of asses, so a similar crossing for a different beast

explanation.surface: A university compared with a famous stumbling block in geometry.
explanation.walkthrough: Pons asinorum, Latin for 'bridge of asses', is Euclid's theorem on isosceles triangles; swap the ass for an ox and you get OX BRIDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxbridge is the collective name for Oxford and Cambridge, used as shorthand for elite British higher education.

clue.text: 6 x 1 20 winks at 14th non-U housebreaker: they're equally responsible

parts.note: six times one, read as six of one; the symbol after it, apparently an ampersand giving and, is missing from the source text
forty winks is a doze, so twenty is half of one
N is the fourteenth letter of the alphabet
a bit of the other is a coarse, non-U phrase for sex, which can break up a home

explanation.surface: A sleepy burglar dozing on a fourteenth-floor job, with blame shared all round.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap after '6 x 1' seems to have held an ampersand, giving AND. Non-U is Nancy Mitford's label for vulgar, not upper-class, speech.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb means two choices or parties are equivalent, so neither side deserves more blame than the other.

clue.text: Nepalese lady in health resort

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: a spa is a resort with healing waters
pronoun for a woman

explanation.surface: A woman from Nepal staying at a spa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lady' is just a pronoun here, not a title; a health resort is the standard crossword spa.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sherpas are a Himalayan people of Nepal, famous as mountaineering guides and porters.

clue.text: Dog has day at last

parts.note: abbreviation of Friday
the end comes at last

explanation.surface: Every dog has its day, the saying goes, and this one finally gets it.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue riffs on the proverb 'every dog has its day'. A dog is proverbially man's best friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Dog stands for a loyal companion, from the saying that a dog is man's best friend.

clue.text: Ill-directed boast regarding attire

indicators.note: something pointed the wrong way faces backwards, so the word is read from the end

parts.note: to boast is to brag

explanation.surface: A misplaced bit of bragging about one's clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Garb is clothing of a distinctive kind, a close synonym of dress or attire.

clue.text: See 18
See 24
Low's TUC was in the wrong order

parts.note: surface reading: a trade union body run by someone named Low; setter's reading: how a cartoonist drew that body
surface reading: muddled; setter's reading: the grid puts the first part above the second, the proverbial wrong way round

explanation.surface: The trade unions under someone's leadership were in a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: The cartoonist David Low drew the TUC (Trades Union Congress, Britain's union federation) as a big, plodding draught animal. Putting the cart before the horse means doing things in the wrong order, as 24 sits before 23 here.
explanation.definitionFit: Low's cartoons pictured the Trades Union Congress as a heavy draught animal, strong but slow and docile.

clue.text: Art's model? That's one way to look at it

indicators.text: one way to look at it
indicators.note: a way of looking at something is a different arrangement of it, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Is this a model in an art class? That's one possible interpretation.
explanation.walkthrough: The same words are both the definition and the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: An old master is a great European painter of the past, whose work serves as an exemplar for art.

clue.text: English lake could give one a turn

parts.note: standard abbreviation
one of the Great Lakes of North America

explanation.surface: A lake in England whose waters might send a boat spinning.
explanation.walkthrough: To give someone a turn is to startle or frighten them.
explanation.definitionFit: Something eerie is uncanny and spooky, so it might frighten or startle a person.

clue.text: Labour could be more than satisfied without the Guardian

definitions.note: the answer describes labour, as in the phrase sweated labour

indicators.note: without here means outside, so one word wraps around the other

parts.note: sated is satisfied to excess
the editorial we, the voice in which a newspaper speaks

explanation.surface: The Labour Party might be very content without the support of this newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks like the political party; it is labour as work. 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but means outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweated labour is underpaid work done in harsh sweatshop conditions, so labour can be described this way.

clue.text: Medal struck without hesitation from stone

indicators.note: something struck is knocked about, so its letters are jumbled
without here means on the outside, wrapping around another piece

parts.note: the anagram of this word
the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A medal minted without any hesitation from a precious stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without hesitation' reads as 'promptly', but 'without' means outside the hesitation sound.
explanation.definitionFit: An emerald is a green precious gemstone, a variety of beryl, so it is a stone.
